Objects 25 26 | Object | What it is | 27 |---|---| 28 | **Workspace** | Top container: projects, issues, agents, members | 29 | **Project** | A group of issues. Has a **lead** — a human OR an agent. Also carries **status · priority · start/due date · icon** (the icon is the only visual marker in lists — use it to tell a product from a recurring pipeline) and **free progress counters** `issue_count` / `done_count` / `resource_count` — read them instead of computing progress yourself | 30 | **Issue** | A unit of work. May have **sub-issues** (one nesting level). Carries native **start date · due date · priority**, plus **`creator_id`/`creator_type`** (the platform already records *whether a human or an agent* made it), **labels**, **KV `metadata`**, **typed `properties`**, board `position`, and both an `identifier` (`ABC-123`) and a `number` — don't confuse the two in scripts | 31 | **Sub-issue** | A child task with one executor; its **`stage`** number groups it into a barrier | 32 | **Agent** | An autonomous worker (model + skills + instructions + runtime) | 33 | **Squad** | A group of agents with one **leader**. Assigned *as a squad*, the leader **routes and does not implement**; the same agent assigned **directly** does its own craft — routing is a mode, not a separate career. Has its own **instructions** (routing rules the leader reads every run) and **avatar**; **`squad delete` archives rather than destroys**, and archiving hands its open issues to the leader so nothing goes silent | 34 | **Project resource** | **Two types exist, verified against the CLI**: `--type` documents `github_repo` and `local_directory`, and `--url` is accepted only for the former — no GitLab, Gitea or self-hosted git today, so say that plainly rather than "I haven't checked". (`--ref` takes a generic JSON payload, so the server may accept more than the CLI exposes; that is a question for the vendor, not a guess to act on.) What a project's agents work on: **`github_repo`** (cloned per task into an isolated worktree → unlimited parallelism) or **`local_directory`** (a folder on one daemon's machine, **serialized by a per-directory lock** — one task at a time, forever; max one per project+daemon) | 35 | **Task** | One agent run (queued → dispatched → running → completed/failed); every trigger = a new task | 36 37 The hierarchy is exactly two levels: `issue → sub-issues`. `stage` is a number on a 38 sub-issue, not another level. 39 40 **Native primitives worth reaching for before writing your own.** 41 42 - **Typed custom properties.** `property create --type text|number|select|multi_select|date|checkbox|url` 43 (coloured options, an icon, **20 active per workspace** — platform cap, not printed by 44 `--help`; **re-verified behaviourally 2026-08-01** — the 21st is refused in the platform's own 45 words: *"a workspace cannot have more than 20 active properties; archive unused ones first"*, 46 so **archiving is the release valve and it preserves values**: a field set may change with the 47 phase of the company rather than being chosen once forever. Two consequences to state before 48 spending the budget — **the cap is per workspace, not per project**, so a methodology field is 49 paid for by every project in the company including those that never use it; and **only an owner 50 or admin may create one**, which makes deploying a field set a step with a person in it rather 51 than something an agent does along the way), values set with 52 `issue property`. **Agents read and write them with validation** — so *Severity*, *Environment* 53 or *Channel* becomes a field, not a sentence buried in a description that every agent parses 54 differently. Prefer a property over prose whenever something is later filtered or counted. 55 - **An agent has fewer fields than a role needs, and where the rest goes is not a matter of 56 taste.** The platform gives `--description`, `--instructions`, `--model`, `--runtime-id`, 57 `--skills`, `--mcp-config`, `--custom-env`, `--max-concurrent-tasks`, `--permission-mode`. 58 It has **no field for type, grade, autonomy or the evidence behind them** — and the temptation 59 is to put them all in the instructions, which is the one place they must not go. 60 61 | What | Where | Why not elsewhere | 62 |---|---|---| 63 | **type** (worker · expert · persona · human) and **grade** | **`--description`** | it is a **routing fact** — what the squad leader reads when deciding whom to `@`-mention. It describes the agent *to others* | 64 | **how the craft is practised** — its rules, its definition of done | **`--instructions`** | this is what the agent reads *about itself*, and it should be about the work | 65 | **autonomy — which gates it clears unasked, and the runs behind that** | **a decision record**, keyed by agent name — plus, where it is real, **`--permission-mode`** and **what is absent from `--custom-env`** | there is no field for it, and a claim about trust belongs where its evidence is | 66 67 **Grade never enters the instructions as an identity.** *"You are a junior engineer"* is not 68 metadata, it is a behavioural instruction, and a model told it is junior acts junior. The 69 leader needs to know the grade; the agent does not need to be told who it is. **The 70 description is read by whoever routes; the instructions are read by whoever works.** 71 72 **And the enforceable half is not a field at all.** Autonomy written into instructions is a 73 request; autonomy expressed as *this agent's environment has no deploy credentials* is a fact 74 — measured 2026-08-01, five of five runs stopped at the missing capability and none invented 75 a way past it. 76 77 - **The inbox is a human channel with rules that decide whether anyone hears you.** It is 78 *"not a full activity log — it flags where something changed that needs your attention"*, and 79 it collects assignments and reassignments, changes to **subscribed** issues (comments, status, 80 priority, dates, assignee), `@`-mentions, reactions to what you created, agent run failures 81 and autopilot activity. **Agents never read it** — there is no CLI surface for it at all. 82 83 **Three of its rules change how a flow must be built:** 84 85 1. **"Your own actions don't notify you."** So an autopilot that files a finding as an issue 86 **notifies nobody by creating it** — it is the author. This is precisely why 87 `autopilot create --subscriber ` exists, and why *"run it in `create_issue` mode"* 88 is only half the instruction: **the other half is naming who is subscribed**, or the 89 auditor reports into an empty room. 90 2. **Notifications on one issue merge into one entry.** A quiet issue and a frantic one look 91 the same in the list, so **the inbox tells you *where* to look, never *how much* happened** 92 — the activity is on the issue. 93 3. **Each group can be switched off** (Settings → Notifications: assignments · status changes · 94 comments and mentions · priority and dates · agent activity). **So "the owner will see it" 95 is an assumption about their settings**, not a property of the system, and anything that 96 must not be missed needs a second channel rather than a louder first one. 97 98 **Subscription is the dial, and it has a CLI while the inbox does not.** 99 `issue subscriber add | list | remove` — *"defaults to the caller"* — so an agent **can 100 subscribe and unsubscribe itself and others**, and **unsubscribing is a real act with a real 101 consequence**: it silences a channel for a person who may be relying on it. Auto-subscription 102 is generous (creating, being assigned, commenting, being mentioned) and **reassignment does 103 not unsubscribe**, so the list grows quietly and a noisy issue is usually an over-subscribed 104 one rather than a busy one. **Two rules follow.** Removing *yourself* is ordinary hygiene. 105 **Removing *someone else* is not** — it is taking them off a thread they were told about, and 106 it is the owner's call, said out loud, not a tidy-up an agent performs while reducing noise. 107 108 **The tension between this and the documentation was a guess; it is now measured.** The docs 109 list *agent run failures* and *autopilot activity* among inbox sources, while this skill said 110 an autopilot task **posts nothing to the inbox**. Both modes were run 2026-08-01 (PLAYBOOKS → 111 *The audit is dispatched*), and what differs is what exists to be notified about, not the 112 channel: **`create_issue` creates a subscribable object**, and the member named in 113 `--subscriber` lands on the issue with `reason: "autopilot"` alongside the agent's own 114 `reason: "creator"`; **`run_only` creates nothing** — the entire answer sits in 115 `autopilot runs → result.output`, and the `--subscriber` that mode accepts without complaint 116 has no issue to attach to. So the instruction is unchanged and now has a reason: 117 `create_issue`, with a named subscriber. **Still unmeasured: a *failing* autopilot** — whether 118 the failure itself reaches a subscriber, or only the issue's existence did. 119 120 - **Removing things: the verbs differ per entity, and the CLI is not the UI.** There is no single 121 *delete*, and assuming one is how a cleanup reports success it did not have. 122 123 | Entity | CLI | Note | 124 |---|---|---| 125 | **project · skill · autopilot · label** | `delete` | actually gone | 126 | **squad** | `delete` — **and its own help says *(archive)*** | the word is delete, the effect is archival | 127 | **agent · property** | `archive` only | reversible (`agent restore`, `property unarchive`); a property's **values are preserved**, and archiving is what frees a slot against the cap of 20 | 128 | **issue** | **none** | `update --status cancelled` is the CLI's whole answer — **the UI has *Delete issue***, so a person can do what an agent cannot | 129 | **workspace** | **none** | the UI has *Delete workspace*; from the console it is not deletable | 130 | **attachment** | **none** | `download` and `upload` only | 131 132 **So `opsinist`'s deletion law lands here with teeth rather than as advice**: *enumerate every 133 destination before removing anything, and name what cannot be deleted at all.* On this 134 platform that list is not rhetorical — an agent asked to *"delete this project"* **cannot** 135 remove the issues or the workspace, and saying *"done"* would be false. 1	# Commands
2	
3	**You never need a command** — plain language in any language works; Mops parses intent and
4	asks when ambiguous. **Every command is namespaced** (`/multica-ops:<verb>`) because that is
5	how plugin commands work: the prefix is what stops two plugins colliding over one verb. There
6	is **no bare `/<verb>`**, and outside Claude Code there are no slash commands at all.
7	
8	**Three doors accept the same opening sentence, and the order is fixed.** *Something is broken*
9	goes to **`bug`** when it is a defect in the product and reproducible — that lane jumps the queue.
10	*Someone told us something* goes to **`mops feedback`**, which triages into accept · decline with
11	a reason · duplicate · snooze. **`report`** is for everything else that went wrong, including
12	when you cannot tell which of the two it is — **it decides from the evidence and may route into
13	`bug` itself, but never skips `feedback`'s triage on the way.**
14	
15	**Nineteen doors, and the palette is the point.** A verb earns a door when it is **its own
16	flow, reached by name, repeatedly** — never as a synonym for another door, and never as a
17	phase inside one. Everything else is **a sentence to the dispatcher**, which costs nothing to
18	keep and is listed further down so the capability stays findable.
19	
20	**`/multica-ops:mops <anything>`** is that dispatcher: free text, any language, any of the
21	flows below (`/multica-ops:mops brand`, `/multica-ops:mops move crossfeed to the next release`).
22	*Where* column: 🖥️ console (heavy/machine/interactive) · 🏢 Mops in Multica (presence/async) ·
23	⇆ either.
24	
25	## The nineteen
26	
27	| Command | Where | Routes to |
28	|---|---|---|
29	| `/multica-ops:mops <anything>` | ⇆ | **the front door** — free text, or nothing at all: day zero, then read what you have and route. Also the way to every flow in *Everything else* below |
30	| `/multica-ops:init` | 🖥️ | bootstrap from zero: **day zero** (BOOTSTRAP §0) → three routing questions → shaping → interview → stand up. Full procedure: FLOWS |
31	| `/multica-ops:join` | 🖥️ | join an existing setup — audit + interview delta, then gaps → fixes; reconcile an existing Mops in Multica. Full procedure: FLOWS |
32	| `/multica-ops:import` | 🖥️ | bring a backlog in from another tracker (Linear, Jira, GitHub Issues, Trello, CSV): extract → show the mapping → create parents then children, **unassigned**, with `source_id` in metadata so a rerun resumes. **Its own door because declaring a crossing turns on two rules** — the mapping is shown before anything is written, and the imported text is treated as untrusted. PLAYBOOKS |
33	| `/multica-ops:quick <task>` | 🖥️ | **the quick-job shape, direct** — 3 questions (deliverable · repo · language), 1–2 agents, build → review, **none of the company machinery**; whatever it outgrows is added later |
34	| `/multica-ops:consult [who] <question>` | ⇆ | **a question, not a build**: answered as an advisor with **zero standing footprint** — no workspace, issue, team or doc created, nothing persisted unless you ask. Address Mops (default), any team agent, an expert, or the theatre. *Nothing will be created* is worth being able to demand. Full flow: FLOWS |
35	| `/multica-ops:status` | ⇆ | the console read, opening with a **countable state line** ("3 need you · 2 running · 4 closed since Tuesday"), then two parts that differ in kind: **needs you** — open requests with their **age and what the wait costs**, staying until answered — and **happened** — events since your last look, ageing out by themselves. Drift is reported separately. Plus spend and **ripe deferrals**; **offered unprompted when you return after time away** |
36	| `/multica-ops:next` | ⇆ | start the next feature from ROADMAP.md — the manual flow's main button |
37	| `/multica-ops:feature <text>` | ⇆ | add a feature mid-flight — raw description is fine: the conductor grills you into a spec → **ICE** against the backlog → proposed release slot → your approval → queued. Too fuzzy to spec? It offers discovery first |
38	| `/multica-ops:ship [release]` | 🖥️ | the **go-live step — whatever "live" means here**: ship code, launch a flavour, publish an episode, send the batch. Gates green → release → notes → tag → announce (deploy and announce are outward → **owner-confirmed**); writes the **cost/effort ledger** and marks it shipped |
39	| `/multica-ops:bug <text>` | ⇆ | the **urgent lane that jumps the queue** — a defect, recall or correction. Minimal spec → **Build (first sub-step: a reproduction / pass-fail signal, before any fix) + Review**, owner notified; not ICE-prioritized |

# Commands

**You never need a command** — plain language in any language works; Mops parses intent and
asks when ambiguous. **Every command is namespaced** (`/multica-ops:<verb>`) because that is

is **no bare `/<verb>`**, and outside Claude Code there are no slash commands at all.

goes to **`bug`** when it is a defect in the product and reproducible — that lane jumps the queue.
*Someone told us something* goes to **`mops feedback`**, which triages into accept · decline with
